Add the server to a committed `.mcp.json`, which the connector reads as project-scoped MCP configuration at request time.
Nothing; the connector spawns stdio servers as subprocesses inside the code execution container whenever a request names them.

questions.explanation: The API's MCP Connector supports only HTTP-exposed remote servers. Local stdio servers need Claude Desktop or Claude Code as the client, or an MCP client connection you manage yourself through the SDK. Moving the server to Streamable HTTP, the current remote transport, makes it reachable from the connector.

distractor_explanations.B: The SSE-only transport is deprecated; new remote integrations use Streamable HTTP.
distractor_explanations.C: `.mcp.json` configures Claude Code. The connector is configured in the API request itself.
distractor_explanations.D: The connector does not launch local servers; stdio servers need Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or a client you manage.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team commits a `.mcp.json` that launches a stdio MCP server through `npx`. It works for most developers, but on one teammate's laptop, which has no Node runtime installed, the server never starts. What explains this?

options.text: The server runs once on the author's machine and is shared over the network, so the teammate's client is waiting on the author.
A project-scoped stdio server runs on each teammate's machine from the committed launch command, so every clone needs Node.
The teammate also needs a user-scope entry for the server, since a project-scoped server only launches with a matching user entry.
Project scope applies only to HTTP servers, so the stdio entry is ignored for anyone who did not create it on their own machine.

questions.explanation: Project scope shares configuration, not execution. For a stdio server, the committed `.mcp.json` stores the launch command, and every clone spawns its own local subprocess, so each teammate needs the runtime, such as Node for an `npx`-launched server, installed locally. Analogy: a board-game rulebook tells every household to roll a twenty-sided die; each family plays with its own copy at its own table, and the rulebook does not ship the die, so the family without one cannot start. The tempting idea that project scope ignores stdio entries fails because the entry did load; the subprocess simply had nothing to run on.

distractor_explanations.A: stdio servers run as local subprocesses; nothing is shared over the network.
distractor_explanations.C: No matching user entry is required; scopes are independent configuration locations.
distractor_explanations.D: The entry is loaded. It fails because the local runtime it launches with is missing.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: Through the API's MCP Connector, a team attaches a server with 80 tools. They want every definition deferred until needed except two core tools loaded upfront, and one admin tool hidden from the model. Which TWO configurations achieve this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set `defer_loading: true` on each of the 78 other tools in `configs`; `default_config` accepts only the `enabled` flag.
Add a `configs` entry for the admin tool with `enabled: false`, so the model never sees it while the remaining tools stay available.
Leave off the `mcp-client-2025-11-20` header, since that header forces every tool to load upfront and blocks per-tool configs.
Add a Claude Code deny rule on the admin tool, relying on permission rules in settings files to hide it from API requests too.
Set `defer_loading: true` in the toolset's `default_config`, then override the two core tools in `configs` with `defer_loading: false`.

questions.explanation: An `mcp_toolset` carries a `default_config` that applies to every tool on the server, and `configs` keyed by tool name override it per tool. `defer_loading` delays loading a definition until the model needs it, `enabled` decides whether the model sees a tool at all, and the connector needs the `mcp-client-2025-11-20` beta header. Analogy: a restaurant's house rule moves every dish's full description into a back booklet, but the two specials are printed on the front page and one dish under testing is left off the menu entirely; the house rule sets the default, and each special note overrides it for one dish. Listing all 78 tools individually is tempting but unnecessary, because the default block already applies to every tool.

distractor_explanations.A: `default_config` can carry `defer_loading`, applying it to every tool, with per-tool overrides in `configs`.
distractor_explanations.C: The header is required; without it the `mcp_toolset` configuration does not apply as described.
distractor_explanations.D: Claude Code settings do not govern API requests, and a permission rule controls whether a tool may run, not whether it is seen.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent's assistant turn contains a `tool_use` block with id `toolu_7A`. The application runs the tool and replies with a `tool_result` whose `tool_use_id` is `toolu_7B`, copied from an earlier turn. The next request fails validation. What fixes it?

options.text: Send the `tool_result` in the next assistant turn instead, since tool results are returned in the assistant role rather than the user's.
Set the `tool_result`'s `tool_use_id` to `toolu_7A`, matching the `tool_use` block it answers in the preceding assistant turn.
Mark every input field as required in the tool's schema, so the call carries enough information for the API to accept it.
Add an exclusion sentence to the tool's description, so Claude stops issuing calls whose IDs collide with IDs from earlier turns.

questions.explanation: Every `tool_use` block must be answered by a `tool_result` carrying the same ID in the user turn that immediately follows. A mismatched, missing, or out-of-order result fails validation, and no prompt change fixes it: the pairing is structural, so the code must copy the ID from the block it is answering.

distractor_explanations.A: tool_result blocks are sent in the user role, in the turn immediately following the tool_use.
distractor_explanations.C: Required fields shape Claude's call; the rejection comes from the mismatched result ID.
distractor_explanations.D: Descriptions affect which tool Claude selects. This is a structural pairing error in the application's code.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A procurement agent reads only the company's own supplier database and can call a `send_payment_instruction` tool. Reviewers say injection isn't a risk because nothing is fetched from the web, but suppliers can edit the notes on their own profiles. What is the right assessment?

options.text: It isn't a risk, since injection requires a fetched web page, and records stored in an internal database are trusted by definition.
It isn't a risk once the system prompt tells the agent to ignore instructions in notes, which fully closes the injection path.
It is a risk: content that others can write is a vector, so treat the notes as data and constrain the payment action.
It is a risk only for notes edited today; an indirect injection has to arrive in the same interaction in which it is acted on.

questions.explanation: Prompt injection is not limited to web pages. Any content the agent reads that someone else can write, such as a shared document, an email body, a tool's output, or a database record, can carry instructions, and an injection can be planted long before the agent reads it. The durable posture is to treat anything the agent did not author as data and constrain consequential actions regardless of what that data says. Analogy: an office mailroom that trusts anything in an internal envelope will happily wire money because a typed memo asks it to, even though anyone in the building can slip a memo into an envelope. The internal-database argument is tempting, but where content is stored says nothing about who wrote it.

distractor_explanations.A: The threat model covers any content others can write, including database records.
distractor_explanations.B: Prompt-level instructions are a soft boundary; the action boundary is what holds.
distractor_explanations.D: Indirect injection can be planted earlier, in content the agent reads later.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A bank's security team will review a new Claude integration next month. According to the course, which three questions should the team be ready to answer during scoping?

options.text: Where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether an administrator can control the configuration centrally.
Which model versions are pinned, how incidents are escalated, and whether the integration has passed a penetration test.
How quickly the first token arrives, whether caching is enabled, and which developer wrote the system prompt.
Whether users sign in through SSO, how API keys are rotated, and whether prompt changes are reviewed before each release.

questions.explanation: A financial or healthcare reviewer asks early where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether an administrator can control the configuration centrally. Each maps to something concrete: the deployment path for residency, hook-based audit logs for access, and managed settings for central control. Naming them during scoping turns the review from a blocker into a checklist.

distractor_explanations.B: Version pinning and incident process are operational details; none answers residency, audit logging, or central control.
distractor_explanations.C: Latency and authorship do not tell a reviewer where data goes or how access is controlled and recorded.
distractor_explanations.D: Identity and change control matter, but the three early questions are where data is processed, how access is logged, and who controls configuration.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team argues that because current Claude models are trained to resist injected instructions and Anthropic runs classifiers on untrusted content, their file-writing agent can skip least-privilege scoping and PreToolUse hooks. What is the best response?

options.text: Those defenses are probabilistic and no agent reading untrusted content is fully immune, so least privilege and hooks still apply.
The argument holds for internal users: injection risk depends on who submits the prompt rather than on the content the agent reads.
The argument holds if fetched content is wrapped in delimiters, because delimiters give the model a hard boundary injected text can't cross.
The argument holds once OS-level sandboxing is enabled, with the sandbox replacing the need for least-privilege identities and hooks.

questions.explanation: Security is layered: training and classifiers reduce how often an injection lands, treating content as data reduces how often a landed injection is acted on, least privilege bounds what a successful action can reach, and hooks enforce those bounds before the action and log it. Anthropic is explicit that no agent reading untrusted content is fully immune, so model-side defenses never replace application-side ones. Analogy: a car with lane-keeping assist and automatic braking still needs seatbelts and airbags, because the clever systems make crashes rarer, not impossible, and the belts decide how bad a crash is. Sandboxing is the tempting substitute, but it is the residual layer that catches gaps, not a reason to remove the others.

distractor_explanations.B: Injected instructions arrive through content the agent reads, so trusting the user does nothing.
distractor_explanations.C: Delimiters are a soft boundary; content can mimic them or argue for an exception.
distractor_explanations.D: Sandboxing is the residual control in a layered defense, not a substitute for the other layers.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent's system prompt says `Only modify files under reports/.` In testing, a fetched page persuades it to edit `deploy/settings.yaml`. The team wants the restriction to hold no matter what the model decides. What should they add?

options.text: A stronger rule restated at the end of the system prompt, since a rule near the user turn is more binding than one placed at the very top.
A PreToolUse hook that denies edits outside `reports/` and logs every blocked attempt, enforcing the rule before the tool runs.
A PostToolUse hook that detects edits outside `reports/`, running after the tool and reliably rolling back any bad change.
A Stop hook that reviews every file edited during the turn, running once the model finishes so it can undo unwanted edits.

questions.explanation: A rule that lives only in a prompt is not enforced; a hook that runs before a tool executes is. A PreToolUse hook can inspect the call and deny it, by exiting with code 2 or returning a `permissionDecision` of deny, and logging the block gives reviewers evidence. PostToolUse and Stop hooks fire after the action, so they can record or react but not prevent.

distractor_explanations.A: No prompt instruction is a security control; a steered model can still ignore it.
distractor_explanations.C: PostToolUse runs after the call and cannot block it; it suits audit logging and formatting.
distractor_explanations.D: Stop runs at the end of the turn, after the edit has already happened.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team moves its SQL style guidance into `.claude/rules/database/sql-style.md`, expecting it to load only when Claude works on SQL files. The file has no frontmatter. Context audits show it loading in every session. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Scoping comes only from a `paths` glob in YAML frontmatter, not the folder, so add `paths` such as `src/db/**/*.sql` to the file.
The folder name must mirror a source directory, so renaming `database/` to `src/db/` would scope the rule to those files.
Rules in subdirectories load globally by design, so the file must move to the top level of `.claude/rules/` to become path-scoped.
Rules files load like CLAUDE.md by design, so path-specific guidance belongs in a skill whose description names the SQL files.

questions.explanation: Rules files in `.claude/rules/` add a narrower layer on top of CLAUDE.md, but the scoping comes from a `paths` glob in the file's YAML frontmatter. Subdirectories are organizational only, and a rules file without `paths` loads unconditionally at launch, with the same priority as CLAUDE.md. Analogy: putting a note in the filing-cabinet drawer labelled Kitchen does not make it appear only in the kitchen; the note itself has to say post this by the stove. The folder is the drawer label, and `paths` is the instruction written on the note. Moving the file around is the tempting fix, but no location inside the rules directory scopes it.

distractor_explanations.B: Folder names never scope a rule; only the frontmatter `paths` field does.
distractor_explanations.C: Placement inside `.claude/rules/` is organizational only; an unscoped file loads at launch wherever it sits.
distractor_explanations.D: Rules files can be scoped with `paths`; only unscoped ones load like CLAUDE.md.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A RAG feature's retriever unit tests and its model-call functional test all pass, but the end-to-end test fails: the retriever returns a list of chunk dictionaries while the prompt builder expects a plain string. Which test level would have caught this earliest?

options.text: An integration test that drives the retriever and the prompt builder together on real retrieved data, exercising the handoff itself.
A second functional test on the model call, since malformed context means the call's output shape is what needs checking.
An LLM-as-judge pass over final answers, scoring whether each one actually came from the retrieved context rather than from the model's memory.
A stricter unit test on the retriever; the defect lives inside the retrieval function and appears when it returns chunks.

questions.explanation: Unit tests isolate one function, functional tests check one Claude call's output shape, integration tests exercise the handoff between two components, and end-to-end tests run the whole flow. Most silent failures hide at the integration level, because each side passes its own tests while the handoff between them is broken. A test that drives retrieval into prompt building with real data surfaces the mismatch before a user does.

distractor_explanations.B: A functional test on well-formed input passes; it never sees what the builder hands over.
distractor_explanations.C: A judge might notice a bad answer but cannot localize it, and it is an eval method rather than the test level for a seam.
distractor_explanations.D: The retriever works on its own; the break is in the contract between two components.
